gloss: say, speak; say in the heart, think; command
summary: The Hebrew Bible's ordinary verb of saying: it introduces nearly every reported speech, from "And God said" at creation to the prophets' "Thus says Yahweh". What is said may be spoken to another, said "in the heart" as thought or resolve, or spoken with authority as a command. Its nouns name what is said, and אִמְרָה above all names Yahweh's word, called refined and trusted as his promise. Aramaic, Syriac and Phoenician share the sense "say", Arabic has "command" and Ge'ez "show, make known"; Akkadian and Ugaritic have a verb ʾmr "see", which may be the same root.

senses.definition: Utter words to someone, the words themselves usually quoted. This is the verb's commonest use, reporting speech throughout narrative, law and prophecy.

evidence.note: "And God said, Let there be light": the words said follow directly.
"You shall say this to the sons of Israel": words given to be passed on.

senses.definition: The infinitive לֵאמֹר, "saying", marks the start of quoted words after another verb of speaking or asking, much as a colon or quotation mark does.

evidence.note: וַיְדַבֵּר יַהְוֶה אֶל־מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר: "And Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying".
After שָׁאַל, "asked ... saying".

senses.gloss: say in the heart: think, resolve
senses.definition: Words "said in the heart" are unspoken thoughts or resolves, reported as speech.

evidence.note: Abraham laughed and said in his heart, "Will a child be born to a man a hundred years old?"
"The fool says in his heart, No God."
"Say in your heart on your bed, and be silent": meditate.

senses.definition: Followed by an infinitive, to say to do something is to purpose it.

evidence.note: "Are you saying to kill me?": do you mean to kill me?
"Behold, I am saying to build a house for the name of Yahweh": I intend to build.

senses.definition: When the speaker has authority, what he says is an order; with an infinitive, to say that something be done.

evidence.note: "He said, and it came to be; he commanded (צִוָּה), and it stood": אָמַר stands in parallel with צִוָּה.
The king "said to" his eunuchs "to bring Vashti".
"Was it not I who said to number the people?"

senses.definition: Of words that are said, or will be said, about someone or something.

evidence.note: "Therefore it is said, Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before Yahweh."

senses.definition: To have a name said of one: to be called.

evidence.note: "Your name will no longer be said (יֵאָמֵר) Jacob, but Israel."
Where "it was said to them, You are not my people", "it will be said to them, Sons of the living God".

senses.definition: Used only of the covenant's two declarations in Deuteronomy 26: Israel has declared Yahweh to be their God, and Yahweh has declared Israel to be his people.

evidence.note: "Yahweh you have declared (הֶאֱמַרְתָּ) today to be your God."
"Yahweh has declared you (הֶאֱמִירְךָ) today to be his people."

senses.definition: Its one occurrence stands with words for arrogant speech, and is read from them: evildoers who "pour out, speak arrogance" are said to יִתְאַמְּרוּ.

evidence.note: "God who said (ὁ εἰπών), Light shall shine out of darkness" takes up Gen 1:3.
"Do not say (μὴ εἴπῃς) in your heart" takes up Deu 9:4 and 30:12.
"Where it was said (ἐρρήθη) to them" takes up the niphal of Hos 2:1.
The Septuagint's εἶπεν for וַיֹּאמֶר.
λέγει in "thus says Yahweh".

parallels.note: command: what Yahweh says is what he commands.
speak: the two are joined as "he spoke ... saying".

phrases.gloss: thus says Yahweh: the messenger's formula introducing a prophet's message

words.summary: Mostly poetic, and most often Yahweh's own word. BDB also lists the same occurrences under the spelling אֶמְרָה.

senses.definition: What someone says, set beside their voice or teaching.

evidence.note: "Hear my voice ... give ear to my saying": קוֹל // אִמְרָה.
"My teaching ... my saying" (לִקְחִי // אִמְרָתִי).

senses.definition: Yahweh's spoken word, refined like tested silver; what he has said and will keep, so that the psalmist waits on it as promise.

evidence.note: "The word of Yahweh is refined."
"Every word of God is refined."
"Your word has given me life": comfort in affliction.
"My eyes fail for your word": waiting for what he said.
"He sends his word to the earth": his word as command.

senses.definition: What is said; in the plural, someone's words or sayings, often set beside other words for speech and instruction.

evidence.note: "There is no utterance (אֹמֶר) and there are no words (דְּבָרִים)".
"Listen to my words (דְּבָרַי); incline your ear to my sayings (אֲמָרַי)."
"the words of God".

senses.definition: A word that sets something in motion or binds: Yahweh gives the word, a man decrees a thing, a promise may seem to fail.

evidence.note: "The Lord gives the word."
"You will decree a thing (תִגְזַר־אוֹמֶר) and it will stand."
"Has his word come to an end?"

words.summary: Found only in Esther, of the king's, Mordecai's and Esther's commands.

senses.definition: An order given by one with authority.

evidence.note: Vashti did not do "the command of King Ahasuerus".
"The decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim."

words.summary: A name built on the verb: "Yah has said". Also spelled אֲמַרְיָהוּ.

senses.gloss: Amariah, a name of several men
senses.definition: Borne by several men, among them priests in the line of Aaron and a chief priest in Jehoshaphat's day.

evidence.note: In the high-priestly line.
"Amariah the chief priest".

cognates.note: Biblical Aramaic, in Daniel and Ezra, with the same senses as the Hebrew, including command.

evidence.note: "The king answered and said" (עָנֵה ... וְאָמַר).
"He said to heat the furnace": command.

cognates.note: Its senses run as the Hebrew's: say, think, command, and in the passive be said, be called. The Peshitta's New Testament keeps the Hebrew idiom: Paul's "do not say in your heart" is דּלָא תִּאמַר בּלֵבָּך.

evidence.note: Peshitta: "do not say (תִּאמַר) in your heart".
Peshitta: "God who said (דֵּאמַר)".
"to say, speak ... to tell, affirm, assert, intend"; Ethpe. "to be said, told".
"dixit ... putavit ... cogitavit, constituit ... jussit"; Etpe. "dictus est ... appellatus est".

cognates.note: Phoenician and Punic, with the noun ʾmr "word" beside it, as Hebrew has אֹמֶר.

evidence.locator: p. 61, ʾ-M-R I and ʾMR II
evidence.note: "1. SAY; 2. SAY to one's self, THINK"; noun "WORD". Cites KAI 14.2 (Eshmunazor, "saying") and KAI 50.2 ("say to my sister").

cognates.gloss: command, order, bid; (stem II) make someone commander
cognates.note: Arabic keeps the root for speech with authority: أَمْر "command, affair".

evidence.note: "He commanded him; ordered him; bade him; enjoined him."
"He made him, or appointed him, commander, governor, lord, prince, or king."

cognates.note: Ge'ez uses the root of making known, and in another stem (አእመረ) of knowing.

evidence.note: "monstrare, ostendere, significare, indicare ... notum facere alicui, edocere"; II,1 "cognoscere, nosse, scire".
"show, indicate, tell, make a sign, make known, demonstrate, inform, instruct".

cognates.gloss: see, look at; find; read (a tablet)
cognates.note: The ordinary Akkadian verb "see", attested more than twelve thousand times in Oracc's corpora, with the root ʾmr; it is never used of speaking. Whether it is the Hebrew root depends on a development "see / be clear > show > say", which the Ge'ez "show, make known" would bridge; Brockelmann counts ʾmr "say" common Semitic "except Akkadian and Ethiopic".

evidence.note: "to see, behold, look at ... to find ... to read (a tablet, a document, an inscription)".
Guide word "see"; root ʾmr.
"(SEM exc. Acc et Aeth)".

cognates.note: Attested as "see" (KTU 1.2 I 32), with Akkadian; no use as "say" was found. Its relation to the Hebrew is the Akkadian's question. Still to consult: DULAT, and Sanmartín, "Semantisches über ʾmr/'Sehen' und ʾmr/'Sagen' im Ugaritischen", UF 5 (1973) 263–270.

evidence.note: "ʾmr Gt: 'see, look at'", compared with Ge'ez ʾammara "show, indicate".
Lists Ugaritic ʾmr "see".

doctrine.statement: In the account of creation each work begins with God's saying, and what he says comes to be: "And God said, Let there be light, and there was light" (Gen 1:3), and so through the days (Gen 1:6, 1:9). The Psalm draws it together: "he said, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood" (Psa 33:9). Paul takes the first of these sayings for the new creation: the God who said light should shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts, to give the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2Co 4:6).

What a person "says in his heart" is treated as speech that God hears and judges. Israel is told not to say in their heart that their own strength won their wealth (Deu 8:17), or that their righteousness won them the land (Deu 9:4). The fool "says in his heart, No God" (Psa 14:1); the king of Babylon "said in his heart, I will ascend to the heavens", and is brought down to Sheol (Isa 14:13, 15). Paul takes up Moses's "do not say in your heart" to set the righteousness of faith against a righteousness of one's own (Rom 10:6, from Deu 9:4 and 30:12).

Yahweh's אִמְרָה, his spoken word, is said to be refined like tested silver (Psa 12:7; 18:31; Pro 30:5), and the psalmist lives by it as promise: it gives him life in affliction (Psa 119:50), he waits for it until his eyes fail (Psa 119:82), and he stores it in his heart so as not to sin (Psa 119:11).

note: Left out, for their own entries: אָמִיר "top, bough" (Isa 17:6, 9), which Wiktionary links to Proto-Semitic *rayam- "be high"; Hos 4:7 אָמִיר, the Hiphil of מוּר "exchange" (as the reader analyses it, with MACULA's lemma and the LXX's θήσομαι), which only the spelling index files here; אֱמֹרִי "Amorite", a people's name; אִמֵּר, אִמְרִי and אוֹמָר, names whose link to the verb is uncertain (names will have their own entries, linking back to their roots); and the unrelated words BDB's section also holds (אֶמֶשׁ, אָנָּא, אֹן, אַמְרָפֶל, אִמַּר "lamb"). BDB's אֶמְרָה is the same word as אִמְרָה (the same occurrences). Ugaritic: DULAT not consulted (no open copy found); worth checking if a copy turns up. Daniel's Aramaic is a cognate here, not a separate word, because the entry is the Hebrew root's.
